SACRAMENTO, CA — Today, the California State Legislature passed Assembly Bill (AB) 1924, statewide legislation poised to address a critical part of California’s homelessness epidemic by preventing displacement before it occurs. Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) and Sharon Quirk-Silva (D-Fullerton), the bill directs the state to build California’s first comprehensive homelessness prevention strategy, complete with measurable goals, accountability benchmarks, and model best practices that cities and counties can use as guidance. AB 1924 passed the State Senate by a 40-0 vote, and the State Assembly by a vote of 77-1.
The numbers behind this bill make the case. Nearly 190,000 Californians are experiencing homelessness, and for every person who exits it, nearly three more fall into homelessness for the first time — a ratio that climbs to 4-to-1 in regions like Los Angeles County. California has invested significant dollars into shelters and housing to catch people after they fall. AB 1924 directs the state to spend that money more efficiently, by keeping people from falling in the first place.
“The best way to reduce homelessness is to keep more Californians housed,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). “We know that prevention is the most humane, compassionate, and cost-effective approach to this crisis and its long past time California adopted a statewide strategy. This legislation will implement a proven strategy and require real accountability so we can finally start to move the needle on this terrible crisis.”
“California cannot solve homelessness by waiting until someone has already lost their home. We must do more to keep people housed in the first place, especially when timely support can prevent a family from losing everything,” said Assemblymember Sharon Quirk-Silva (D-Fullerton). “AB 1924 gives California a stronger framework to identify what works, coordinate prevention efforts, and measure whether we are reaching the people who need help before they enter homelessness. Thank you, Assemblymember Gabriel, for ensuring California is smarter with our resources and giving families a better chance to remain safely and securely housed.”
Proof of Concept Already Exists
Prevention is not a theory. Homelessness prevention programs are already established in Santa Clara County, Sonoma County, and elsewhere throughout the state. Innovative programs like homelessness prevention units, which predict who is most likely to become homeless and intervene before help is sought, demonstrate what the future of prevention could look like. What has been missing is a statewide framework to connect these efforts, measure what works, and scale it statewide.
AB 1924 gives the state a way to connect the dots. The bill requires the California Interagency Council on Homelessness to develop a statewide homelessness prevention strategy, including goals and accountability measures. It directs relevant state agencies to build their own homelessness prevention action plans, and requires the state to identify and disseminate evidence-based model practices that local governments and service providers can adopt.
What Experts and Community Leaders Are Saying
"Preventing homelessness is much more humane and vastly less expensive than waiting to react to it. Yet for all California's investments on homelessness, the state has done little to prevent it in the first place. This bill makes prevention a strategic priority, moving California toward the cutting edge of nationwide efforts to solve our homelessness crisis.” — Mike Feuer, Senior Policy Advisor at Inner City Law Center
"We've seen prevention programs in the Bay Area and Los Angeles start turning the tide on people becoming homeless. This bill would direct California to develop a statewide strategy to implement these critical programs for the first time. Independent researchers have proven how effective homelessness prevention can be at keeping people housed even months after they received assistance, and we hope the state will build off this experience to bring these programs statewide." — Brett Andrews, Interim CEO of All Home
“The best way to end homelessness is to stop it before it starts. Prevention is not only the most compassionate approach, it is also cost-effective, proven to work, and gives families a chance to stay safely housed before a crisis becomes a catastrophe. California has an opportunity right now to make prevention a priority through AB 1924 and take a meaningful first step toward helping thousands of families stay in their homes." — Jennifer Loving, CEO of Destination: Home
What’s Next
The legislation now heads to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk, where he will have until September 30 to decide whether to veto the bill or sign it into law.

SACRAMENTO, CA — Earlier this week, the California State Legislature passed Assembly Bill (AB) 1836, legislation that would better protect communities facing hate-motivated violence. Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) and Chris Ward (D-San Diego), AB 1836 would expand the California State Nonprofit Security Grant Program (NSGP) so nonprofits can use grant funding to secure the events that bring people out into the community, including Pride parades, cultural festivals, public celebrations, and more. AB 1836 passed both houses of the State Legislature with unanimous bipartisan support, and follows a historic win in the State Budget where Assemblymember Gabriel helped to secure $80 million in ongoing annual funding for the NSGP.
“California is stepping up to protect our communities, so that Californians of all faiths and backgrounds can gather together and celebrate without fear,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), Chair of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus. “This bill sends a powerful message that California will continue to stand with the LGBTQ+ community and all others targeted by hate. We will never let hate win.”
“Every Californian deserves to feel safe when they enter a place of worship, walk into a community center, attend a Pride celebration, or gather with their community,” said Assemblymember Chris Ward (D-San Diego), Chair of the California Legislative LGBTQ Caucus. “AB 1836 strengthens California’s commitment to protecting organizations and communities that too often face threats simply because of who they are or who they serve. I am grateful to our legislative colleagues for passing this important legislation and thankful to my friend and fellow Diversity Caucus Chair, Assemblymember Gabriel, for leading the charge. I now urge Governor Newsom to sign AB 1836 into law so we can ensure our LGBTQ+, Jewish, and other communities targeted by hate have the resources they need to gather safely and without fear.”
Closing a Dangerous Gap
Since 2015, the NSGP has helped hundreds of houses of worship, community centers, and reproductive health clinics secure critical security enhancements — but that protection has stopped at the front door. AB 1836 would ensure that organizations at risk of hate-motivated violence could also utilize grant funding for security at offsite events such as Pride Parades and community religious observances, where the risk of hate-motivated violence is often greatest. Recent deadly attacks at a Hanukkah celebration in Sydney and a Pride parade in Berlin are stark reminders of the extreme vulnerability for offsite events.
A Diverse Coalition Built on Shared Safety
AB 1836 is sponsored by Jewish California and Equality California and supported by more than 100 organizations representing LGBTQ+, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, Christian, Latino, and Asian American communities. That breadth and depth of this diverse interfaith coalition reflects a simple truth: that Californians of all faiths and backgrounds must stand together against hate.
"Hate doesn't stop at the doors of a nonprofit organization—and neither should the protections designed to keep our communities safe," said Tony Hoang, Executive Director of Equality California. "From Pride festivals to community gatherings, LGBTQ+ Californians deserve the freedom to celebrate, connect, and access support without fear of harassment or violence. AB 1836 closes a critical gap in California's security infrastructure and reflects the shared commitment of LGBTQ+, Jewish, and other vulnerable communities to ensure that hate never prevents people from coming together. We are proud to partner with Assemblymember Gabriel and Jewish California to advance this important measure."
"Our communities don't just gather behind security doors – we gather for religious holidays in the park, we demonstrate, and we host public festivals and parades," said David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California. "Vulnerable communities should not have to worry about safety when practicing our traditions in the community. But with hate-motivated violence on the rise, the cost of securing these gatherings has become prohibitive for many organizations, threatening the very community-building that defines us. We thank Assemblymember Gabriel for his leadership in solving this problem, and we're proud to work alongside Equality California to make sure every Californian can come together without fear."
A Program Born From Tragedy, Built to Meet Growing Demand
California pioneered the nation’s first dedicated, state-funded Nonprofit Security Grant Program in 2019 with legislation authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel following the deadly shooting at a synagogue in Poway. Over the last several years, the state has committed more than $380 million to the program. Demand for the NSGP has outpaced that investment. In the most recent funding cycle, more than 1,600 organizations applied for grants, making it the most popular grant program administered by the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES).
What’s Next
The legislation now heads to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk, where he will have until September 30 to decide whether to veto the bill or sign it into law.

SACRAMENTO, CA — Yesterday, the California State Legislature passed Assembly Bill (AB) 395, a nation-leading bill that would promote greater religious and cultural inclusivity by requiring officials to consider important religious and cultural holidays when scheduling public meetings and significant academic milestones. Authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), Chair of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, AB 395 passed both houses of the State Legislature with unanimous bipartisan support.
AB 395 closes a quiet but persistent gap. For years, many Californian families have faced difficult choices between religious observance and full participation in education and civic life, particularly when state agencies and universities have scheduled public meetings, graduations, and other events on holidays such as Diwali, Rosh Hashanah, Eid al-Fitr, and the Feast of the Nativity.
To address this problem, AB 395 would require state agencies to take a proactive approach and make a good faith, reasonable effort to avoid scheduling public meetings on important religious, cultural, or ancestral holidays. The bill extends that same standard to public colleges and universities for significant events like graduation ceremonies, the first day of classes, and other major academic milestones. AB 395 likewise encourages local governments and K-12 school districts to follow suit — helping to promote religious and cultural inclusivity across the Golden State.
“California is immensely proud of our diversity, and Californians of all faiths and backgrounds should be able to fully participate in public life,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). “For too long and in too many communities, religious minorities and other people of faith have been asked to make difficult choices on the days that matter most to them. This legislation would help to prevent that injustice, and ensure that Californians of all backgrounds can fully participate, particularly when important decisions are being made.”
AB 395 was supported by an exceptionally broad and diverse coalition of nearly 80 organizations representing Jewish, Muslim, Christian, Hindu, Armenian, and Zoroastrian communities, as well as labor unions representing teachers, school employees, and government workers.
"AB 395 ends a quiet but persistent form of exclusion — the choice too many Californians have faced between practicing their faith and fully participating in school and civic life,” said David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California. “It's also the first time Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Passover, and other faiths' religious holidays will be recognized in California statute. We thank Assemblymember Gabriel for his leadership, and the remarkably diverse coalition of labor, education, and interfaith partners — including 61 Jewish organizations — who came out in support."
"The passing of AB 395 is a tremendous step forward in achieving true cultural inclusivity and religious freedom in California,” said Salam Al-Marayati, President of the Muslim Public Affairs Council. “The freedom to observe sacred days is critical to maintaining one's religious identity, especially for the children of faith communities who too often must make decisions at a young age between religious expression and not being left out. The Muslim Public Affairs Council is proud to have supported this legislation, and we look forward to continuing in the work where all faith communities feel heard in every space they are in.”
“The Hindu American Foundation is grateful for the passage of Assembly Bill 395. It is an important step toward fostering religious accommodation and civic inclusion in California,” said Samir Kalra, Esq., Managing Director of Policy & Programs at the Hindu American Foundation. “Hindu families frequently face scheduling conflicts that force difficult choices between work or school and significant cultural traditions like Diwali. By establishing guidelines for state entities to respect major cultural observances, this bill ensures that California’s government represents and respects the state's diverse population. We are thankful to Assemblymember Gabriel for his leadership on this important legislation and we look forward to continuing this work with policymakers and community partners.”
What’s Next
The legislation now heads to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk, where he will have until September 30 to decide whether to veto the bill or sign it into law.

SACRAMENTO, CA — Help is on the way for millions of California families trying to decode ingredient lists on packaged foods. Earlier this week, the California Legislature passed Assembly Bill (AB) 2244, landmark legislation designed to empower Californians to make better informed and healthier choices by increasing transparency around ultraprocessed foods. Authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D - Encino), AB 2244 would establish a first-in-the-nation “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal that food manufacturers could place on products that meet clear standards for not being ultra-processed. Modeled after the widely recognized “USDA Organic” label, the seal would provide consumers with a simple, trustworthy way to identify healthier options with a quick glance. The bill also would require grocery stores in California to display products bearing the “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal, thereby making it easier for busy families to find healthier foods quickly and conveniently.
“While Washington D.C. is paralyzed by inaction, Republicans and Democrats in California are joining forces to empower consumers to avoid harmful ultra-processed foods,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D - Encino). “Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives. Parents shouldn't need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids. California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and this week’s vote is the next big step toward protecting our kids from harmful ultra-processed foods.”
A Bipartisan Coalition
AB 2244 passed the Legislature with the support of a broad bipartisan coalition that includes the Environmental Working Group, the California Medical Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Diabetes Association, the American Heart Association, the Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation, and the United Nurses Associations of California. The bill passed the State Senate on a vote of 32-0 and the State Assembly 72-0.
Building on California’s Track Record as the National Leader on Food Safety
AB 2244 is the latest in a series of Gabriel-authored laws that have reshaped how California – and increasingly the country – thinks about what’s in our food. Last year, Assemblymember Gabriel authored and Governor Newsom signed into law The Real Food, Healthy Kids Act (AB 1264, 2025), groundbreaking legislation which established the nation’s first statutory definition of ultra-processed foods and set up a process to ban harmful products from California schools. Assemblymember Gabriel also successfully passed into law two other landmark bills with bipartisan support: the California Food Safety Act (AB 418, 2023) and the California School Food Safety Act (AB 2316, 2024). Collectively, these laws have helped change the national conversation about food additives and ultra-processed foods, shaped federal policy, and inspired similar legislation across more than 30 other states.
The Science Behind the Seal
Research has increasingly linked high consumption of ultra-processed foods to serious health harms, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, Type 2 diabetes, metabolic disorders, reproductive harm, and other chronic conditions. Despite these risks, many consumers struggle to distinguish between minimally processed and highly processed products due to confusing labels and marketing practices.
AB 2244 would address this challenge by creating a simple certification program that would empower consumers with clear, front-of-package information and improve access to healthier options through strategic in-store placement. Modeled after the successful and widely recognized “USDA Organic” label, this legislation would establish a process overseen by the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) where food manufacturers could apply to accredited certification agents to use the “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” label on their packaging, thereby indicating that a product meets clear standards for not being ultra-processed. This seal reflects the same commonsense, market-based approach that made the USDA Organic label a success: give manufacturers a voluntary standard worth meeting, and let consumers do the rest.
Voices Behind the Seal: What Experts and Community Leaders Are Saying
“Once again, California is leading the way by helping consumers identify and avoid UPFs. Last year, California enacted the nation’s first definition of UPFs. This week, California has taken the next step by helping consumers distinguish between processed foods, which are part of a healthy diet, and ultra processed foods, which are engineered to be overeaten. Our food should nourish us, not make us sick. EWG is so grateful that Assemblymember Gabriel is continuing to put our health first.” – Melanie Benesh, Vice President of Government Affairs, Environmental Working Group
“As a dietitian and nutrition researcher, it is clear to me that most people want to choose healthy foods for their kids. But nutrition information is not easy to interpret, and junk foods tend to dominate grocery store shelves. By clearly labeling foods non-ultra-processed and making them easy to find in stores, this bill sets people up for success.” – Alyssa J. Moran, ScD, MPH, Deputy Director, Center for Food and Nutrition Policy, University of Pennsylvania
“We have a long road ahead to a food supply free from harmful chemicals and a healthier America. In the meantime, we must give consumers the tools and knowledge to make healthier food choices. By creating a ‘Non-Ultraprocessed Certified’ seal to help identify healthier, non-UPF options, Assemblymember Gabriel continues to advance California’s leadership in the fight to reduce consumption of the hyperpalatable, addictive ultra-processed foods driving our nation’s chronic disease crisis.” – Todd Wagner, entrepreneur and co-founder of FoodFight USA
What’s Next
The legislation now heads to Governor Gavin Newsom's desk, where he will have until September 30 to decide whether to veto the bill or sign it into law.

SACRAMENTO, CA — Today, the California State Legislature passed The Second Chance Sports Act, bipartisan legislation authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) that would expand access to organized sports programming in California correctional facilities as a strategy to improve public safety, reduce recidivism, and support successful reentry into society. Jointly authored with Assemblymembers Isaac Bryan (D - Los Angeles) and Juan Alanis (R - Modesto), Assembly Bill (AB) 2204 would encourage prisons to use sports as a tool to help incarcerated Californians rehabilitate and successfully return to their communities.
Specifically, this bill would direct the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) to adopt a comprehensive statewide policy to increase opportunities for participation in organized sports for incarcerated persons and authorize CDCR to enter into partnerships with colleges, universities, and professional sports teams and leagues. The bill also would establish a dedicated fund – known as the Second Chance Sports Fund – to support public-private partnerships and expand programming in a targeted and cost-effective manner.
“Sports can be a powerful tool to help incarcerated individuals transform their lives and successfully reintegrate into the community,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D - Encino). “Structured sports programs can help build discipline, teamwork, and accountability. The Second Chance Sports Act will harness the power of sports to promote rehabilitation, support correctional staff, reduce recidivism, and build stronger, safer communities across California. This bipartisan legislation will reduce violence inside our prisons and reduce crime when people return home.”
“Anyone who has played a team sport understands the positive impacts it can have on a person. Playing sports reduces depression and anxiety, provides positive social interaction, and gives people a chance to think about how their actions impact a collective outcome,” said Assemblymember Isaac Bryan (D - Los Angeles), a longtime criminal justice reform advocate and coauthor of AB 2204. “Expanding access to this kind of programming for people who are incarcerated is good for both public safety and rehabilitation.”
“Accountability is only one step in reducing crime and making our communities safer,” said Assemblymember Juan Alanis (R - Modesto), coauthor of AB 2204 and a longtime law enforcement officer. “I believe The Second Chance Sports Act is a positive step toward encouraging rehabilitation, reducing recidivism, and incentivizing the kind of discipline and accountability that makes real second chances possible. Public safety and second chances are not opposing values — they go hand in hand, and this bill reflects that.”
Research has consistently shown that participation in organized sports and other structured programming reduces disciplinary incidents and lowers the likelihood that individuals will reoffend. It also improves physical fitness and mental health and helps individuals to build critical traits like communication skills, discipline, emotional regulation, and self-esteem, which can improve reintegration into society. By expanding access to organized sports – paired with mentorship and clear behavior expectations – this legislation aims to transform idle time into an opportunity for personal growth, responsibility, and rehabilitation.
Proof of concept for this approach already exists in California. The San Quentin Giants – a baseball program at San Quentin that has received support from the San Francisco Giants – provides opportunities for participants to practice against each other as well play games against outside teams and organizations. Participants have spoken publicly about the profound impact the program has had on their rehabilitation and self-esteem. AB 2204 would help to replicate such programming across California’s correctional system.
What Experts and Community Leaders Are Saying
“Many of the things that people look for in gangs, they get out of sports. The camaraderie, the family atmosphere, the feeling of belonging to something. Sports was a way for me to interact with different cultures and learn how to be in heated situations without losing my cool.” - Jacob Brevard, Chief of Programs at the Anti Recidivism Coalition (ARC)
“From a law enforcement perspective, AB 2204 is about promoting what works to make communities safer. Giving people structured opportunities through sports to build discipline and skills while they’re incarcerated helps reduce reoffending — and that’s a win for public safety.” — Sean Thuilliez, President of the California Police Chiefs Association
"California's correctional officers see firsthand the difference that meaningful programming makes — for the people in our facilities and for the safety of our communities. When incarcerated Californians have real opportunities to build discipline, self-esteem, and teamwork, everyone benefits — including our members who work alongside them every day. We're proud to support Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel’s Second Chance Sports Act and we look forward to working with the Legislature to make it a success." — Neil Flood, President of the California Correctional Peace Officers Association (CCPOA)
“While I was incarcerated at Valley State Prison, the Fuego semi-professional soccer team came in as part of a reentry day, and that experience became one of the most impactful moments leading up to my release in 2025. What stood out wasn’t just the game—it was the community they created among all of us who participated. The compassion, understanding, and completely nonjudgmental atmosphere they brought into that space allowed me to witness a side of humanity I hadn’t seen in decades. For the first time in a long time, I saw what healthy, everyday people in a functioning, supportive community actually look like. That moment planted something in me that I didn’t fully understand until after I paroled. It gave me a real, lived example of connection, belonging, and positive engagement that I could carry with me into the world. Since then, I’ve been intentional about building that same kind of community around me—spaces rooted in respect, accountability, and genuine care. I now actively contribute to my community and strive to create healthy networks wherever I go, because I know firsthand the impact that kind of environment can have—not just on me, but on anyone who experiences it.” — Michael Stephens, Advocate with Healing Dialogue and Action
What’s Next
The legislation now heads to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk, where he will have until September 30 to decide whether to veto the bill or sign it into law.

SACRAMENTO, CA — Last week, the California State Legislature passed AB 1626, key legislation that will put mental health and substance use disorder training in the hands of youth sports coaches. Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), Blanca Pacheco (D-Downey), and Jacqui Irwin (D-Thousand Oaks), AB 1626 passed with overwhelming bipartisan support and now heads to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk.
“For many young people, mental health intervention can be the difference between life and death,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). “Coaches are uniquely positioned and are often the first to notice when young people are struggling and in need of help. This bill will empower youth sports coaches with the tools and training they need to help students in crisis.”
“I'm grateful for all the coaches who have helped me build confidence and resilience, on and off the court,” said Stephen Curry, NBA Champion. “Through Eat. Learn. Play., we've seen what's possible when coaches have the training and resources to support a young athlete's well-being, not just their game. Every kid deserves that kind of coach, and we’ve been proud to make investments to ensure coaches in Oakland have the tools to be a great leader. Policies like Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel’s bill help create a strong foundation for coaching practices that can make a lasting impact in an athlete’s life.”
For coaches across California, AB 1626 turns good intentions into real preparation. It requires K-12 sports coaches to complete training on recognizing the warning signs of depression, anxiety, eating disorders, substance use disorders, and suicidal ideation — and on how to connect a struggling student athlete to resources. It also directs the California Department of Education to build a model training that recreational and club coaches statewide can use to do the same.
A Crisis Playing Out on California’s Fields and Courts
The numbers behind AB 1626 tell a stark story. Studies show that teenagers throughout the state are struggling with mental health issues at an increasing rate. More isolated than ever before, California’s young men and boys have experienced an alarming rise in suicide rates and feel more disconnected from school, work, and relationships. Nearly one in four men under 30 report having no close friends at all. Meanwhile, young female athletes face their own elevated risks of depression, anxiety, body image struggles, and eating disorders.
Coaches are often uniquely positioned to catch the warning signs, as they see young athletes for numerous hours each week, through wins, losses, and everything in between — and they’re frequently the first to notice when something is wrong. Yet only one in five coaches report feeling highly confident in their ability to support a student dealing with a mental health or substance use disorder, and four in five say they feel less than fully prepared. Left without guidance, coaches may miss the moment to step in, or at worst, make a difficult situation harder, as stigma keeps students from speaking up.
AB 1626 tackles the problem from both ends: it sets statewide training requirements for K-12 coaches, and it directs the state to build a model training that recreational and club programs can put to use. The goal is simple — to make sure the adults kids already trust are ready to help when it matters most.
Backed by Champions On and Off the Field
AB 1626 is sponsored by the California Alliance of Children and Family Services, Mental Health America of California, the Play Equity Fund, and the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls, and backed by a broad and diverse coalition that includes State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond, the San Francisco Giants, U.S. Soccer Foundation, San Francisco 49ers, NAMI California, the American Academy of Pediatrics of California, the Association of California School Administrators, and dozens of other education, youth, and mental health organizations.
“As we work to address the youth mental health crisis, we must look at the full circle of adults who support our students,” said Assemblywoman Blanca Pacheco (D-Downey). “Coaches are trusted mentors who see student athletes in high-pressure moments, yet many don’t have the tools to respond to mental health challenges. I’m glad to partner on AB 1626, in coordination with my bill, AB 1665, to equip coaches to recognize when a student is struggling and connect them to support.”
“This bill is about turning awareness into life-saving action,” said Assemblywoman Jacqui Irwin (D-Thousand Oaks). “The community I represent in Ventura County lost a remarkable person when the life of Sarah Shulze was tragically cut short by suicide in 2022. Sarah was a talented multi-event runner, and her loss underscores the urgent need to better equip the adults our students trust to recognize and respond to mental health warning signs.”
"We are proud to support AB 1626 and its focus on equipping coaches with the tools to better support the mental health and wellbeing of young athletes. Through our work with partners like CalHOPE, Counseling and Support Services for Youth (CASSY), and Beyond Sport, we've seen firsthand the impact coaches can have on improving mental health outcomes in young people. By further strengthening these relationships and resources across the state, we can help create safer, more supportive environments where every young athlete has the opportunity to thrive." — Justin Prettyman, Executive Vice President, Philanthropy and Executive Director, 49ers Foundation
“I commend Assemblymember Gabriel for recognizing the positive influence of coaches on young athletes, and for introducing AB 1626 to ensure coaches are equipped to support youth mental health and strengthen the connection between physical and emotional health. Coaches play a pivotal role in building relationships and creating team environments that help young people thrive. At a time when many youth face a crisis of isolation and disconnection, coaches can help them feel a sense of belonging.” — Renata Simril, President, Play Equity Fund
“By equipping coaches with the tools to foster supportive team environments, identify mental health risks, and connect student athletes to appropriate professional support, this bill strengthens the safety net around our youth and advances our statewide commitment to serve the whole child and protect school-based wellness and prevention.” — California State Superintendent of Public Instruction, Tony Thurmond
“Our young people don’t experience life in silos, so our support system shouldn’t be either. We must meet youth where they are, and AB 1626 helps us accomplish that. Coaches are on the front lines and notice when there are changes in a student athlete’s behavior, stress, and well-being. Equipping coaches with the appropriate tools to identify, respond, and support youth creates a proactive system of care that is youth-centered and culturally responsive, improving their long-term mental health and wellness. AB 1626 is an important step toward strengthening California’s behavioral health continuum of care for youth and represents the type of investment California urgently needs. Mental Health America of California is grateful for Assemblymember Gabriel’s commitment to reshaping systems of care to reflect the diverse experiences of youth and help close gaps in access to quality services and supports.” — Tiffany Murphy, Chief Operations Officer, Mental Health America of California
“Everyone talks about prevention, but few invest in it. AB 1626 is what prevention looks like in practice. Youth mental health has reached a crisis point, but early identification can change the trajectory of a young person’s life. When a trusted adult, like a high school coach, is trained to recognize when a young athlete is struggling and also knows how to respond, that coach can connect that young athlete with care and, in some cases, save their life. The California Alliance represents more than 200 members who serve children, youth, and families every day, and we're proud to sponsor this common-sense bill and are grateful to Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel for his leadership." — Pete Weldy, Chief Executive Officer, California Alliance of Children and Family Services
What’s Next
The legislation now heads to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk, where he will have until September 30 to decide whether to veto the bill or sign it into law.

SACRAMENTO, CA — With California’s homicide rate at its lowest point in recorded history, California Governor Gavin Newsom took a key step in furthering public safety by signing Assembly Bill (AB) 2378, a bill authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), which establishes an Office of Community Violence Intervention (CVI). This law expands and strengthens the California Violence Intervention and Prevention (CalVIP) Grant Program — the very initiative credited with helping drive that drop in crime. As applications for CalVIP funding continue to pour in at record levels, AB 2378 gives the program the senior-level leadership it needs to keep pace and keep saving lives, using the dedicated funding source established by historic legislation authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, the California Gun Violence Prevention and School Safety Act of 2023.
“California has become a national leader in reducing gun violence because we’ve made a sustained commitment to investing in smart, proven strategies to stop violence before it occurs,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), co-founder of California’s Gun Violence Working Group. “AB 2378 builds on that leadership by creating a dedicated Office of Community Violence Intervention to strengthen and coordinate this lifesaving work across our state. I’m grateful to Governor Newsom for signing this important legislation and for his continued leadership in protecting our communities.”
The numbers tell the story of a state whose approach to public safety is working. Studies show that California’s homicide rate fell to 3.5 per 100,000 residents in 2025, the lowest rate recorded since the state began tracking crime statistics in 1966. Homicides dropped 18.6 percent and the statewide violent crime rate fell 10.2 percent in a single year. Community violence intervention programs like CalVIP, which put trusted messengers directly into neighborhoods most affected by gun violence, have been central to that progress.
Under the Director’s leadership, the Office of CVI will administer the CalVIP program more effectively, coordinate with the Department of Justice’s Office of Gun Violence Prevention, engage in long-term strategic planning, share best practices, evaluate grant implementation, and provide technical support to applicants and grantees.
Why AB 2378 Matters
In 2019, Governor Newsom signed the Break the Cycle of Violence Act, codifying the CalVIP Grant Program. In 2023, he signed the historic California Gun Violence Prevention and School Safety Act, authored by Assemblymember Gabriel, establishing a permanent, dedicated funding source for CalVIP.
The impact has been significant: communities that received CalVIP funding saw homicides decrease nearly three times more than those that did not. In 2024, California recorded its lowest gun homicide rate in state history, driven by sharp reductions in violence among the young people the program is designed to reach. Given this success, demand for CalVIP has surged. During the most recent application cycle, requests for funding topped $1 billion. AB 2378 expands and strengthens critical violence intervention work across California and helps ensure the state’s investment keeps producing results.
AB 2378 was backed by a broad coalition of gun violence prevention advocates, cities, and community-based organizations, including sponsor GIFFORDS, Everytown for Gun Safety, Moms Demand Action, Students Demand Action, and Brady California, along with several others — reflecting diverse perspectives.
What Community Leaders Are Saying
“From Oakland to Los Angeles, California is seeing record-low rates of gun violence. These aren’t just impressive numbers — these are real lives being saved. With the formation of a statewide office of community violence intervention, we will be able to expand and improve on this critical work, creating stronger, healthier communities. Consistent funding through CalVIP is the backbone of gun violence prevention work in our state. By creating this new office, we can ensure that funding is being awarded and distributed by people with firsthand experience, and that every dollar goes toward saving lives.” — Mike McLively, Policy Director at GIFFORDS Center for Violence Intervention
“Community violence intervention programs are a critical part of the work to prevent gun violence and save lives in communities across California, and they deserve strong, coordinated support. AB 2378 will help ensure California’s investments in this lifesaving work are strategic, sustainable, and informed by what works on the ground. We’re grateful to Assemblymember Gabriel for his continued leadership.” — Alex Navarro, Volunteer with the California Chapter of Moms Demand Action

LOS ANGELES, CA — Help is on the way for millions of California families trying to decode ingredient lists on packaged foods. At a bill signing ceremony at UCLA Mattel Children’s Hospital, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill (AB) 2244, landmark legislation that will empower Californians to make better informed and healthier choices by increasing transparency around ultra-processed foods. Authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), AB 2244 establishes the first-ever “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal that food manufacturers can place on products that meet clear standards for not being ultra-processed. Modeled after the widely recognized “USDA Organic” label, the seal will provide consumers with a simple, trustworthy way to identify healthier options with a quick glance. The bill also will require grocery stores in California to prominently display products bearing the “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal, thereby making it easier for busy families to find healthier foods quickly and conveniently.
“While Washington D.C. is paralyzed by inaction, Republicans and Democrats in California are joining forces to empower consumers to avoid harmful ultra-processed foods,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). “Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives. Parents shouldn't need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids. California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and with Governor Newsom’s continued leadership we are taking another big step forward today.”
Building on California’s Track Record as the National Leader on Food Safety
AB 2244 is the latest in a series of Gabriel-authored laws that have reshaped how California – and increasingly the country – thinks about what’s in our food. Last year, Assemblymember Gabriel authored and Governor Newsom signed into law The Real Food, Healthy Kids Act (AB 1264, 2025), groundbreaking legislation which established the nation’s first statutory definition of ultra-processed foods and set up a process to ban harmful products from California schools. Assemblymember Gabriel also successfully passed into law two other landmark bills with bipartisan support: the California Food Safety Act (AB 418, 2023) and the California School Food Safety Act (AB 2316, 2024). Collectively, these laws have helped change the national conversation about food additives and ultra-processed foods, shaped federal policy, and inspired similar legislation across more than 30 other states.
The Science Behind the Seal
Research has increasingly linked high consumption of ultra-processed foods to serious health harms, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, Type 2 diabetes, metabolic disorders, reproductive harm, and other chronic conditions. Despite these risks, many consumers struggle to distinguish between minimally processed and highly processed products due to confusing labels and marketing practices.
AB 2244 addresses this challenge by creating a simple certification program that empowers consumers with clear, front-of-package information and improves access to healthier options through strategic in-store placement. Modeled after the successful and widely recognized “USDA Organic” label, this legislation establishes a process overseen by the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) where food manufacturers could apply to accredited certification agents to use the “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” label on their packaging, thereby indicating that a product meets clear standards for not being ultra-processed. This seal reflects the same commonsense, market-based approach that made the USDA Organic label a success: give manufacturers a voluntary standard worth meeting, and let consumers do the rest.
A Broad and Bipartisan Coalition
AB 2244 passed the Legislature with support of a broad coalition that includes the Environmental Working Group, the California Medical Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Diabetes Association, the American Heart Association, the Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation, and the United Nurses Associations of California. The bill passed with overwhelming bipartisan support with votes of 32-0 in the State Senate and 72-0 in the State Assembly.
Voices Behind the Seal: What Experts and Leaders Are Saying
“Once again, California is leading the way by helping consumers identify and avoid UPFs. Last year, California enacted the nation’s first definition of UPFs. This week, California has taken the next step by helping consumers distinguish between processed foods, which are part of a healthy diet, and ultra processed foods, which are engineered to be overeaten. Our food should nourish us, not make us sick. EWG is so grateful that Assemblymember Gabriel is continuing to put our health first.” – Melanie Benesh, Vice President of Government Affairs, Environmental Working Group
“It’s clear that most Americans are concerned about ultra-processed foods and want to avoid them, but these products are so ubiquitous and heavily promoted that it’s become exceedingly hard to do that. An easy-to-understand front-of-package label makes it so much easier for Californians to choose the non-ultra-processed options they want for their families. This is an important step towards a food supply that prioritizes whole, nourishing foods over industrially produced food products.” – Alyssa J. Moran, ScD, MPH, Deputy Director, Center for Food and Nutrition Policy, University of Pennsylvania
“We have a long road ahead to a food supply free from harmful chemicals and a healthier America. In the meantime, we must give consumers the tools and knowledge to make healthier food choices. By creating a ‘Non-Ultraprocessed Certified’ seal to help identify healthier, non-UPF options, Assemblymember Gabriel and Governor Newsom continue to advance California’s leadership in the fight to reduce consumption of the hyperpalatable, addictive ultra-processed foods driving our nation’s chronic disease crisis.” – Todd Wagner, entrepreneur and co-founder of FoodFight USA

SACRAMENTO, CA — Today, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill (AB) 1924 — statewide legislation poised to address a critical part of California’s homelessness epidemic by preventing displacement before it occurs. Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) and Sharon Quirk-Silva (D-Fullerton), the bill directs the state to build California’s first comprehensive homelessness prevention strategy, complete with measurable goals, accountability benchmarks, and model best practices that cities and counties can use as guidance.
The numbers behind this bill make the case. Nearly 190,000 Californians are experiencing homelessness, and for every person who exits it, nearly three more fall into homelessness for the first time — a ratio that climbs to 4-to-1 in regions like Los Angeles County. California has invested significant dollars into shelters and housing to catch people after they fall. AB 1924 directs the state to spend that money more efficiently, by keeping people from falling in the first place.
“The best way to reduce homelessness is to stop it before it starts,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). “We know that prevention is the most compassionate and effective approach to this crisis, and it’s long past time California adopted a statewide prevention strategy. I’m grateful to Governor Newsom for signing AB 1924 into law and helping us pair proven prevention strategies with real accountability.”
“California cannot solve homelessness by waiting until someone has already lost their home. We must do more to keep people housed in the first place, especially when timely support can prevent a family from losing everything,” said Assemblymember Sharon Quirk-Silva (D-Fullerton). “AB 1924 gives California a stronger framework to identify what works, coordinate prevention efforts, and measure whether we are reaching the people who need help before they enter homelessness. Thank you, Assemblymember Gabriel, for ensuring California is smarter with our resources and giving families a better chance to remain safely and securely housed.”
Proof of Concept Already Exists
Prevention is not a theory. Homelessness prevention programs are already established in Santa Clara County, Sonoma County, and elsewhere throughout the state. Innovative programs like homelessness prevention units, which predict who is most likely to become homeless and intervene before help is sought, demonstrate what the future of prevention could look like. What has been missing is a statewide framework to connect these efforts, measure what works, and scale it statewide.
AB 1924 gives the state a way to connect the dots. This law requires the California Interagency Council on Homelessness to develop a statewide homelessness prevention strategy, including goals and accountability measures. It directs relevant state agencies to build their own homelessness prevention action plans, and requires the state to identify and disseminate evidence-based model practices that local governments and service providers can adopt.
What Experts and Community Leaders Are Saying
“The best way to end homelessness is to stop it before it starts. California is showing compassion and common sense go hand-in-hand by making prevention a strategic priority, moving the state toward the cutting edge of nationwide efforts to solve our homelessness crisis.” — Jennifer Loving, CEO of Destination: Home
“It’s not only much more humane to keep residents in their homes—it’s much less expensive than providing shelter and services once they fall into homelessness. With this bill, prevention becomes a central pillar of California’s homeless policy. If we can begin to move the paradigm to preventing homelessness in the first place, we can finally turn the tide on one of our most intractable challenges.” — Mike Feuer, Senior Policy Advisor at Inner City Law Center
“Targeted homelessness prevention is a strategy that's proven by practice and research, not just theory. We've watched it keep families housed in the Bay Area and Los Angeles for years, and independent researchers have confirmed the results. Now California has the chance to build a statewide system around what we already know works.” — Brett Andrews, Interim CEO of All Home

SACRAMENTO, CA — Today, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed two new laws to safeguard constitutional rights and protect Californians from reckless federal immigration enforcement actions. Authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), Assembly Bill (AB) 1806 and AB 1807 were developed in response to ICE raids in Los Angeles, the deadly violence in Minneapolis, and continued threats from reckless federal immigration enforcement actions across the country.
“California must continue to push back against the Trump Administration to protect our immigrant communities and our constitutional rights,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). “I’m proud that AB 1807 will prohibit federal immigration agents from using state property for immigration enforcement, while AB 1806 will require an independent, transparent, and thorough state investigation when an immigration officer fatally shoots an unarmed civilian. Together, these new laws will strengthen the rule of law and protect the people who call our state home. I’m grateful to Governor Newsom for signing these bills and standing with our communities.”
AB 1806: Requiring Independent Investigations for Immigration-Related Shootings
AB 1806 requires the California Attorney General to conduct an independent, transparent, and thorough investigation into any fatal shooting of an unarmed civilian by an immigration officer, closing an accountability gap that has left families across the country without answers.
That gap has grown more urgent by the day. Since the immigration enforcement surge began in 2025, agents have opened fire on civilians at an unprecedented rate. Studies have identified multiple incidents in which immigration agents fired at or into civilian vehicles, resulting in four deaths. At least five of the people shot were U.S. citizens.
Two cases drew national attention: Renee Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, was fatally shot by an ICE agent in Minneapolis. Alex Pretti, an ICU nurse, was fatally shot by a CBP officer just weeks later. In both cases, the U.S. Department of Justice declined to investigate, and state and local officials say they were blocked from accessing evidence and crime scenes by federal officials.
The pattern has reached California as well. In Northridge, Keith Porter Jr. was shot and killed by an off-duty immigration officer. In case after case, the same agency investigating itself has amounted to no investigation at all, while the Trump Administration has told agents they operate with “federal immunity.”
AB 1806 closes this gap by extending a framework California trusts. It builds on AB 1506 (2020), which requires an independent investigation of deadly police shootings, and extends it to fatal shootings of unarmed civilians by immigration agents. Under AB 1806, the California Attorney General must conduct an independent, transparent and thorough investigation into every shooting of an unarmed civilian. If charges are warranted, the Attorney General must prosecute, and the findings must be made public in a written report.
“As the author of the landmark legislation that created independent investigations into police shootings (AB 1506, 2020), I applaud Assemblymember Gabriel and Governor Newsom for expanding this important accountability measure to include actions by immigration officers through AB 1806.” said Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty.
AB 1807: Preventing ICE Agents from Using State Resources for Immigration Enforcement
Since June 2025, federal immigration agents have repeatedly used California’s own property to launch raids that have terrorized California communities. Immigrants and U.S. citizens alike have been detained in public spaces, at workplaces, and near their homes, often in front of their own children.
AB 1807, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and Assemblymember Juan Carrillo (D-Palmdale), prohibits state-owned property, including parking lots, vacant lots, and garages, from being used to stage, process, detain, or otherwise support federal immigration enforcement operations. It requires state agencies to identify vulnerable properties, post signage, limit access, and develop enforcement procedures to keep unauthorized federal activity off state land.
At its core, AB 1807 draws a boundary so that public property is used to serve California residents, not terrorize them.
“What we are seeing throughout our nation is a result of an administration that has normalized fear, intimidation, and use of force in our communities. That is why I’m proud to stand alongside Assemblymember Gabriel to ensure federal agents do not continue to terrorize immigrant communities and American citizens in our state,” said Assemblymember Juan Carrillo (D-Palmdale), Joint Author of AB 1807 and Chair Elect of the California Legislative Latino Caucus.
A Broad and Diverse Coalition
AB 1806 and AB 1807 were sponsored by the California Immigrant Policy Center and backed by one of the largest Capitol coalitions of the year, which included more than 100 organizations spanning labor, immigrant rights, legal aid, civil rights, and faith communities. Supporters include SEIU California, the California Immigrant Policy Center, the California Democratic Party, the Latino Community Foundation, and local governments from across California.
“No person should die at the hands of any government official or in government custody. The signing of AB 1806 and AB 1807 into law sends a strong message: California will ensure our state resources are used to protect the safety and rights of all Californians — not to facilitate dangerous immigration raids, detentions and deportations,” said Shiu-Ming Cheer, Deputy Director at the California Immigrant Policy Center.

SACRAMENTO, CA — Today, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill (AB) 2020, bipartisan legislation authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) that supports the development and maintenance of affordable housing by enabling builders to use their existing portfolio resources to stabilize at-risk affordable housing developments and protect vulnerable residents who rely on them.
“California’s affordable housing developments currently operate on razor-thin margins,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). “We cannot afford to lose units that took years and significant public investment to create — especially to a foreclosure that could have been prevented. Preserving what we’ve built is far more cost-effective than starting over. AB 2020 gives the state a smart, practical tool that helps keep these properties afloat and keeps vulnerable Californians housed, and I applaud Governor Newsom for his signature on this important measure.”
How AB 2020 Protects Tenants
Affordable housing developments financed by the state are required to remain affordable to low-income households for extended periods, often 55 years or longer, and operate with limited financial margins that depend on carefully structured reserves and operating income to remain solvent over that entire span.
During and after the COVID-19 pandemic, many of these properties were required to draw down operating reserves to offset lost rental income, while insurance, maintenance, and financing costs rose sharply. As a result, a growing number of developments now face operating deficits and heightened foreclosure risk, threatening the permanent loss of affordable units at a time when California can least afford to lose them.
Preserving an existing affordable home is significantly more cost-effective and expeditious than constructing a new one. Until now, state law has not clearly authorized a developer to transfer funds between properties within its own portfolio to prevent such a loss, even when a financially stable building exists alongside a struggling one under common ownership.
AB 2020 addresses this issue head-on. The new law authorizes the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) to approve the transfer of excess reserves or the department’s share of residual receipts between affordable housing developments that share the same sponsor or affiliated ownership and are subject to a departmental regulatory agreement. In practice, this means a builder managing multiple properties can use funds from a financially stable building to stabilize a distressed one within the same portfolio, subject to HCD’s approval on a case-by-case basis.
What Housing Leaders Are Saying
“Preserving the state's existing affordable housing is one of the most cost-effective investments California can make. It is far cheaper to stabilize a distressed property today than to replace it tomorrow. AB 2020 gives housing providers a no-cost tool they can use in partnership with government and private lenders to keep affordable homes stable and performing for the low-income Californians who depend on them. We are grateful to Assemblymember Gabriel for his leadership on this important bill.” — Matt Schwartz, President and CEO of California Housing Partnership
“The rising insurance premiums and other operating cost pressures are threatening the sustainability and viability of affordable housing providers. AB 2020 represents a targeted tool to protect the long-term stability of affordable housing, ensuring Californians can remain in their homes and communities. We are grateful to Assemblymember Gabriel and his office for their leadership on this important effort.” — Jimar Wilson, Enterprise Community Partners Vice President and Southern California Market Leader
"Affordable properties that fall into distress do not fail suddenly. Their stability erodes over several years as insurance, maintenance, and financing costs increase, and the moment to intervene is well before a recapitalization becomes the only option. AB 2020 gives HCD a targeted way to act early without touching the payment rights of any city, county, or housing authority. For our members operating older properties with thin margins, that flexibility can be the difference between a stable building and losing affordable homes that we have all worked so diligently to create. We thank Assemblymember Gabriel for advancing a practical fix at a moment when the sector needs every tool available to keep homes affordable for low-income Californians.” — J.T. Harechmak, Policy Director, Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California (NPH)
“This is a common-sense change that is critical to the long-term stability of, not only California's supply of affordable homes, but the long-term stability of rural, agricultural, and Native communities and families. Assemblymember Gabriel's leadership on this issue was key to moving this critical policy.” — Alicia HF Sebastian, Executive Director of the California Coalition for Rural Housing

SACRAMENTO, CA — Today, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill (AB) 395, nation-leading legislation that promotes greater religious and cultural inclusivity by requiring officials to consider important religious and cultural holidays when scheduling public meetings and significant academic milestones. Authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), Chair of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, AB 395 passed both houses of the State Legislature with unanimous bipartisan support.
AB 395 closes a quiet but persistent gap. For years, many California families have faced difficult choices between religious observance and full participation in education and civic life, particularly when state agencies and universities have scheduled public meetings, graduations, and other events on holidays such as Diwali, Rosh Hashanah, Eid al-Fitr, and the Feast of the Nativity.
To address this problem, AB 395 requires state agencies to take a proactive approach and make a good faith, reasonable effort to avoid scheduling public meetings on important religious, cultural, or ancestral holidays. The new law extends that same standard to public colleges and universities for significant events like graduation ceremonies, the first day of classes, and other major academic milestones. AB 395 likewise encourages local governments and K-12 school districts to follow suit — helping to promote religious and cultural inclusivity across the Golden State.
“Californians of all faiths and backgrounds should be able to fully participate in public life,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), Chair of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus and the author of AB 395. “California is proud of our extraordinary diversity, but for too long members of our religious communities have been forced to choose between observing their faith and participating in important public events and academic milestones. This new law will help remove those barriers and ensure that Californians of all backgrounds can fully participate in civic and academic life. We are grateful to the diverse, interfaith coalition that championed this effort and to Governor Newsom for signing this important legislation.”
AB 395 was supported by an exceptionally broad and diverse coalition of nearly 80 organizations representing Jewish, Muslim, Christian, Hindu, Armenian, and Zoroastrian communities, as well as labor unions representing teachers, school employees, and government workers.
"AB 395 ends a quiet but persistent form of exclusion — the choice too many Californians have faced between practicing their faith and fully participating in school and civic life,” said David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California. “It's also the first time Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Passover, and other faiths' religious holidays will be recognized in California statute. We thank Governor Newsom for his signature, Assemblymember Gabriel for his leadership, and the remarkably diverse coalition of labor, education, and interfaith partners — including 61 Jewish organizations — who came out in support."
"The passing of AB 395 is a tremendous step forward in achieving true cultural inclusivity and religious freedom in California,” said Salam Al-Marayati, President of the Muslim Public Affairs Council. “The freedom to observe sacred days is critical to maintaining one's religious identity, especially for the children of faith communities who too often must make decisions at a young age between religious expression and not being left out. The Muslim Public Affairs Council is proud to have supported this legislation, and we look forward to continuing in the work where all faith communities feel heard in every space they are in.”
“Assembly Bill 395 is an important step toward fostering religious accommodation and civic inclusion in California. The Hindu American Foundation is grateful to Governor Newsom for signing AB 395 into law and appreciates Assemblymember Gabriel’s leadership in advancing it, said Samir Kalra, Esq., Managing Director of Policy & Programs at the Hindu American Foundation. “Scheduling conflicts regularly compel Hindu families to choose between their education or livelihoods and sacred observances like Diwali. This legislation ensures that state public institutions respect and accommodate California's rich cultural diversity.”

SACRAMENTO, CA — Yesterday, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed The Second Chance Sports Act, bipartisan legislation authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) that will expand organized sports programming in California correctional facilities as a strategy to improve public safety, reduce recidivism, and support successful reentry into society. Jointly authored with Assemblymembers Isaac Bryan (D-Los Angeles) and Juan Alanis (R-Modesto), Assembly Bill (AB) 2204 directs the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) to adopt a comprehensive statewide policy to increase opportunities for participation in organized sports for incarcerated persons and authorizes CDCR to enter into partnerships with colleges, universities, and professional sports teams and leagues. The bill also establishes a dedicated fund – known as the Second Chance Sports Fund – to support public-private partnerships and expand programming in a targeted and cost-effective manner.
“Sports can be a powerful tool to help people transform their lives and successfully reintegrate into their communities,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). “The Second Chance Sports Act will harness the power of sports to teach discipline, teamwork, and accountability, reduce violence inside our prisons, and help reduce crime when people return home. I’m grateful to the bipartisan coalition of law enforcement leaders and criminal justice reform advocates who came together around this commonsense approach to building stronger, safer communities, and to Governor Newsom for signing this bill into law.”
Research has consistently shown that participation in organized sports and other structured programming reduces disciplinary incidents and lowers the likelihood that individuals will reoffend. It also improves physical fitness and mental health and helps individuals to build critical traits like communication skills, discipline, emotional regulation, and self-esteem, which can improve reintegration into society. By expanding access to organized sports – paired with mentorship and clear behavior expectations – this legislation aims to transform idle time into an opportunity for personal growth, responsibility, and rehabilitation.
Proof of concept for this approach already exists in California. The San Quentin Giants – a baseball program at San Quentin that has received support from the San Francisco Giants – provides opportunities for participants to practice against each other as well as play games against outside teams and organizations. Participants have spoken publicly about the profound impact the program has had on their rehabilitation and self-esteem. AB 2204 will help to replicate such programming across California’s correctional system.
What Experts and Community Leaders Are Saying
“Anyone who has played a team sport understands the positive impacts it can have on a person. Playing sports reduces depression and anxiety, provides positive social interaction, and gives people a chance to think about how their actions impact a collective outcome,” said Assemblymember Isaac Bryan (D-Los Angeles), a longtime criminal justice reform advocate and co-author of AB 2204. “Expanding access to this kind of programming for people who are incarcerated is good for both public safety and rehabilitation.”
“Accountability is only one step in reducing crime and making our communities safer,” said Assemblymember Juan Alanis (R-Modesto), a longtime law enforcement officer and co-author of AB 2204. “I believe The Second Chance Sports Act is a positive step toward encouraging rehabilitation, reducing recidivism, and incentivizing the kind of discipline and accountability that makes real second chances possible. Public safety and second chances are not opposing values — they go hand in hand, and this bill reflects that.”
“From a law enforcement perspective, AB 2204 is about promoting what works to make communities safer. Giving people structured opportunities through sports to build discipline and skills while they’re incarcerated helps reduce reoffending — and that’s a win for public safety.” — Sean Thuilliez, President of the California Police Chiefs Association
“Many of the things that people look for in gangs, they get out of sports. The camaraderie, the family atmosphere, the feeling of belonging to something. Sports was a way for me to interact with different cultures and learn how to be in heated situations without losing my cool.” — Jacob Brevard, Chief of Programs at the Anti Recidivism Coalition (ARC)
"California's correctional officers see firsthand the difference that meaningful programming makes — for the people in our facilities and for the safety of our communities. When incarcerated Californians have real opportunities to build discipline, self-esteem, and teamwork, everyone benefits — including our members who work alongside them every day. We're proud to support Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel’s Second Chance Sports Act and we look forward to working with the Legislature to make it a success." — Neil Flood, President of the California Correctional Peace Officers Association (CCPOA)
"I've seen firsthand what sports can do for a kid with nothing to hold onto. This law is about giving people a real shot at redemption, and I can't think of anything more worth fighting for.” — T.Y. McGill, Former NFL Player and NFL Players Coalition Ambassador
“While I was incarcerated at Valley State Prison, the Fuego semi-professional soccer team came in as part of a reentry day, and that experience became one of the most impactful moments leading up to my release in 2025. What stood out wasn’t just the game—it was the community they created among all of us who participated. The compassion, understanding, and completely nonjudgmental atmosphere they brought into that space allowed me to witness a side of humanity I hadn’t seen in decades. For the first time in a long time, I saw what healthy, everyday people in a functioning, supportive community actually look like. That moment planted something in me that I didn’t fully understand until after I paroled. It gave me a real, lived example of connection, belonging, and positive engagement that I could carry with me into the world. Since then, I’ve been intentional about building that same kind of community around me—spaces rooted in respect, accountability, and genuine care. I now actively contribute to my community and strive to create healthy networks wherever I go, because I know firsthand the impact that kind of environment can have—not just on me, but on anyone who experiences it.” — Michael Stephens, Advocate with Healing Dialogue and Action
